Cranial Nerves and Brainstem - I
Aftab Merchant, MBBS, FCPS, MHPE
Professor of Medical Education
Assistant Dean of Anatomical Education
Kirk Kerkorian School of Medicine
University of Nevada Las Vegas

Learning Objectives
1. Describe the external anatomy of the brainstem, including the midbrain, pons, medulla, major surface
landmarks, cranial nerve attachment sites, and major arterial supply. (CLO 1)
2. Describe the anatomical pathways, functional components, and major functions of the twelve cranial
nerves, including their passage through skull foramina and clinically relevant head and neck structures,
and correlate peripheral cranial nerve lesions with their characteristic neurological deficits. (CLO 1,
CLO 2, CLO 3)
3. Explain the internal organization of the brainstem, including the arrangement of cranial nerve nuclei,
cranial nerve fascicles, major ascending and descending pathways, and vascular territories, and
describe their roles in normal sensory, motor, and autonomic function. (CLO 1, CLO 2)

Cranial Nerve Organization
Functional Components • Brainstem Nuclei • Pathways

Cranial Nerve Functional Components
Abbreviation Functional Component General Function
Motor
GSE General somatic efferent Motor to skeletal muscles derived from somites
SVE Special visceral efferent Motor to pharyngeal arch muscles
GVE General visceral efferent Parasympathetic motor to glands, heart, and smooth muscle
Sensory
SVA Special visceral afferent Smell, taste
GVA General visceral afferent Sensory input from viscera
GSA General somatic afferent General sensations – touch, pain, temperature
SSA Special somatic afferent Vision, hearing, balance
Efferent = motor output | Afferent = sensory input

Organization of Cranial Nerve Nuclei
• Motor nuclei → medial
• Sensory nuclei → lateral
• Motor and sensory columns are separated by the sulcus limitans
• Functional columns follow a predictable medial-to-lateral organization
Motor = medial | Sensory = lateral
GVA + SVA share the solitary nucleus: SVA mainly rostral; GVA mainly caudal.
Dorsal brainstem view showing sensory (left) and motor (right) cranial nerve
nuclei; matching colors indicate common embryologic origin.
Neuroanatomy. Crossman, 7e.

Cranial Nerve Nuclei by Level
Midbrain: III, IV
Pons: V, VI, VII, VIII
Medulla: IX, X, XII
Spinal Cord: XI
Don't memorize every nucleus on this map. Use it to identify the
brainstem level and recognize that some nuclei extend across levels.

Eye Movements & Ocular Motor Nerves
CN III • CN IV • CN VI • Extraocular Muscles • Peripheral Lesions

Extraocular Muscle Innervation
• CN III: medial rectus, superior rectus, inferior rectus, inferior oblique
• CN IV: superior oblique
• CN VI: lateral rectus
• CN III: levator palpebrae superioris
LR6 • SO4 • All others III
Fig. 8.92 Gray’s Anatomy for Students, 3e.

Anatomical Actions vs Clinical Testing Watch the video:
https://youtu.be/3J2UZiLVZKA?feature=shared
• Extraocular muscles have multiple anatomical actions
• Clinical testing positions the eye to preferentially isolate a muscle’s vertical action
Anatomical Actions Clinical Testing
Recti: abduct first | Obliques: adduct first
Anatomical actions describe muscle biomechanics; clinical
testing describes how muscle function is isolated on examination.

Extraocular Muscles: Actions & Testing
Muscle Primary Clinical Test
Medial rectus Adduct
Lateral rectus Abduct
Superior rectus Abduct → elevate
Inferior rectus Abduct → depress
Superior oblique Adduct → depress
Inferior oblique Adduct → elevate
Recti tested in abduction | Obliques tested in adduction
Fig. 8.92 Gray’s Anatomy for Students, 3e.

Oculomotor Nerve (CN III)
• Origin: midbrain
• Oculomotor nucleus (GSE) → most extraocular muscles + levator palpebrae
• Edinger–Westphal nucleus (GVE) → parasympathetic fibers
• Passes through cavernous sinus → superior orbital fissure
• Parasympathetic: Edinger-Westphal → ciliary ganglion → short ciliary nerves
• Controls: sphincter pupillae → miosis | Ciliary muscle → accommodation
Fig. 12.61A. Origin and distribution of the oculomotor nerve. Wineski, SCABR, 10e.
Champney. ECNA, 2016.
Fig. 12.61A. Origin and distribution of the oculomotor nerve. Wineski, SCABR, 10e.

Oculomotor Nerve Palsy
• Eye “down and out”
• Ptosis
• Mydriasis
• Loss of accommodation
• Diplopia
Pupil Involvement Fig. B8.31A Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 9e.
• Compressive lesion → pupil often involved (dilated)
• Ischemic lesion → pupil often spared
CN III palsy → Ptosis + 3Ds
(Down + Deviated + Dilated pupil)
Fig. 8.92 Gray’s Anatomy for Students, 3e.

Trochlear Nerve (CN IV)
• Origin: midbrain
• Motor (GSE) → superior oblique
• Only CN that exits dorsally
• Fibers decussate before exiting
• Passes through cavernous sinus → superior orbital fissure
• Superior oblique: intorsion + depression in adduction
Fig. 8.99 Gray’s Anatomy for Students, 3e.
CN IV → superior oblique → “down and in” testing
CN IV nucleus lesion → contralateral superior oblique weakness
CN IV nerve lesion → ipsilateral superior oblique weakness

Trochlear Nerve Palsy
• Vertical/torsional diplopia
• Worse looking down and in
• Difficulty descending stairs or reading
• Affected eye tends to be elevated and extorted
• Compensatory head tilt away from lesion
CN IV palsy → trouble looking down when the eye is adducted

Abducens Nerve (CN VI)
• Origin: pons
• Motor (GSE) → lateral rectus
• Passes through cavernous sinus → superior orbital fissure
• Lateral rectus abducts the eye
CN VI → lateral rectus → abduction

Abducens Nerve Palsy
• Lateral rectus paralysis
• Eye pulled medially (esotropia)
• Horizontal diplopia
• Worse looking toward the affected side
• Compensatory head turn toward lesion
Fig. B8.31B Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 9e.
CN VI palsy → cannot abduct the affected eye

Facial Sensation & Movement
CN V • CN VII • Facial Sensation • Facial Movement • Corneal Reflex

Trigeminal Nerve (CN V)
• Origin: pons
• Major sensory nerve of the face
• V1 Ophthalmic: sensory
• V2 Maxillary: sensory
• V3 Mandibular: sensory + branchial motor (SVE)
• V3 motor → muscles of mastication
V1 + V2 = sensory | V3 = sensory + motor

Trigeminal Divisions & Skull Foramina
• V1 Ophthalmic → superior orbital fissure
• V2 Maxillary → foramen rotundum
• V3 Mandibular → foramen ovale
Fig 8.284. Gray’s Anatomy for Students, 3e.

Trigeminal Sensory Nuclei
• Mesencephalic nucleus: proprioception
• Principal (chief) sensory nucleus: fine touch & vibration
• Spinal trigeminal nucleus: pain & temperature
Midbrain → proprioception | Pons → touch | Caudal → pain & temperature
Champney. ECNA, 2016.
Dorsal brainstem view of the cranial nerve nuclei. Crossman, 7e.

Trigeminal Motor Function
• Motor nucleus of CN V: pons
• V3 (SVE) → muscles of mastication
• Masseter, temporalis, medial & lateral pterygoids
• LMN lesion → weakness of ipsilateral mastication
• Jaw deviates toward the weak side on opening
Masseter Temporalis
V3 LMN Lesion →
jaw deviates toward the weak side on opening
Medial Pterygoid Lateral Pterygoid
Fig. 8.137, 8.139, 8.142, 8.143. GAS, 3e.

Facial Nerve (CN VII)
• Origin: pons
• SVE: muscles of facial expression
• GVE: lacrimal, submandibular & sublingual glands
• SVA: taste from anterior 2/3 of tongue
• GSA: small area of external ear
• Travels through internal acoustic meatus → facial canal
• Exits skull through stylomastoid foramen
CN VII = facial movement + parasympathetic + taste
Facial nerve anatomy.
UpToDate, 2019.

Facial Nerve: Major Branches
• Greater petrosal nerve → lacrimal/nasal/palatal glands
• Nerve to stapedius
• Chorda tympani → taste anterior 2/3 + salivary parasympathetics
• Motor branches → muscles of facial expression
Lesion location determines which CN VII functions are lost
Facial nerve anatomy.
UpToDate, 2019.

Central vs Peripheral Facial Weakness
Corticobulbar Innervation
• Most cranial motor nuclei receive bilateral cortical input
• Important exceptions: lower facial motor neurons (CN VII) and genioglossus
motor neuron (CN XII) receive predominantly contralateral input
UMN Lesion
• Contralateral lower-face weakness
• Forehead relatively spared
• Upper face receives bilateral cortical input
LMN / CN VII Lesion
• Ipsilateral upper + lower-face weakness
• Forehead not spared
Bell Palsy
Forehead spared → UMN | Entire ipsilateral face weak → LMN
Bell palsy = peripheral CN VII (LMN) palsy
Singh. TCNA, 3e.

Corneal (Blink) Reflex
• Corneal touch activates V1 (nasociliary branch)
• Afferent limb: CN V1
• Efferent limb: CN VII
• CN VII → orbicularis oculi → eyelid closure
• Normal response: bilateral blink
Corneal reflex: V1 in → VII out
Figure 11.4 A: Corneal reflex.
Splittgerber, SCNA, 8e.

Hearing & Balance
CN VIII • Cochlear Division • Vestibular Division • Clinical Correlates

Vestibulocochlear Nerve (CN VIII)
• Origin/attachment: pontomedullary junction
• Special somatic afferent (SSA)
• Cochlear division → hearing
• Vestibular division → balance & head movement
• Enters internal acoustic meatus (IAM) with CN VII
• Sensory nuclei extend across the pons–medulla region
CN VIII = SSA → hearing + balance
Fig. 8.123 Gray’s Anatomy for Students, 3e.

CN VIII: Cochlear vs Vestibular
Cochlear Division
• Sensory input from the cochlea
• Function → hearing
• Terminates in cochlear nuclei
• Lesion → sensorineural hearing loss ± tinnitus
Vestibular Division
• Sensory input from the vestibular apparatus
• Function → balance & head movement
• Terminates in vestibular nuclei
• Lesion → vertigo, nystagmus, imbalance
Fig. 8.124 Gray’s Anatomy for Students, 3e.
Cochlear → hearing | Vestibular → balance

Vestibular Schwannoma
• Schwann-cell tumor, usually arising from the vestibular division of CN VIII
• Often begins within the internal acoustic meatus
• CN VIII: unilateral sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, imbalance
• May extend into the cerebellopontine angle (CPA)
• Larger tumors may compress adjacent CN VII and CN V
• Acoustic neuroma is a historical misnomer
The anatomy of cerebellopontine angle (CPA).
Kościołek, Biomedicines. 2024

Ménière’s Disease (Endolymphatic Hydrops)
• Disorder of the inner ear caused by excess endolymph in the membranous labyrinth.
• Increased endolymph pressure → distention of cochlear and vestibular membranes
→ dysfunction of hair cells.
Clinical Triad
• Vertigo (recurrent, episodic)
• Tinnitus (ringing or roaring in the ear)
• Fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss (usually unilateral early)
Additional Features
• Sensation of ear fullness or pressure
• Symptoms may be triggered by stress, tiredness (fatigue), illness, dietary factor
Image: Medline Plus

Pharynx, Larynx & Visceral Function
CN IX • CN X • Swallowing • Phonation • Gag Reflex • Visceral Function

Glossopharyngeal Nerve (CN IX)
• Origin: medulla
• SVE: stylopharyngeus → swallowing
• GVE: parotid gland
• SVA: taste from posterior 1/3 of tongue
• GVA: carotid sinus & carotid body
• GSA: posterior 1/3 tongue, oropharynx & middle ear
• Exits skull through jugular foramen
Fig. 11.17. Distribution of the glossopharyngeal nerve.
CN IX = posterior 1/3 tongue + carotid sinus/body + stylopharyngeus + parotid
Images: Champney; Splittgerber, SNA, 8e

Vagus Nerve (CN X)
• Origin: medulla
• SVE: most muscles of soft palate, pharynx & larynx
• GVE: parasympathetic to thoracic & abdominal viscera
• SVA: taste from epiglottis/posterior tongue
• GVA: thoracic & abdominal viscera
• GSA: pharynx, larynx & external ear
• Exits skull through jugular foramen
CN X = swallowing + phonation + visceral parasympathetic
Fig. 12.65. Distribution of the vagus nerve.
Wineski, SCABR, 10e.

CN IX & X: Key Brainstem Nuclei
Motor (Efferent)
• Nucleus ambiguus (SVE) → pharyngeal/laryngeal motor
• Inferior salivatory nucleus (GVE) → CN IX → parotid gland
• Dorsal motor nucleus of X (GVE) → thoracoabdominal viscera
Sensory (Afferent)
• Nucleus solitarius (GVA & SVA) → taste & visceral sensory input
• Spinal trigeminal nucleus (GSA) → somatic sensation
Ambiguus = motor | Dorsal motor X = parasympathetic | Solitarius = sensory
Dorsal brainstem view of the cranial nerve nuclei. Crossman, 7e.

Vagus Motor Function & Lesion
• Weakness of palate, pharynx & larynx
• Dysphagia
• Hoarseness
• Impaired efferent limb of gag reflex
• Palate droops on affected side
• Uvula deviates away from the lesion
CN X lesion → palate droops ipsilaterally; uvula points away
Singh. Neurosciences, 2015.

Pharyngeal (Gag) Reflex
• Touch posterior pharynx → bilateral pharyngeal contraction
• Afferent limb: CN IX
• Efferent limb: CN X
• Motor response → pharyngeal elevation/contraction
Gag reflex: IX in → X out
Fig. 8.205 GAS, 4e.

Larynx Innervation (CN X)
Superior Laryngeal Nerve
• External laryngeal nerve: motor → cricothyroid
• Internal laryngeal nerve: sensory → above cords
Inferior (Recurrent) Laryngeal Nerve
• Motor → all laryngeal muscles except cricothyroid
• Sensory → below vocal folds
Right RLN → loops under right SCA
Left RLN → loops under aortic arch
Fig. 8.221, 8.228 Gray’s Anatomy for Students, 4e.
46

Head, Neck & Tongue Motor Function
CN XI • CN XII • Head & Shoulder Movement • Tongue Movement

Accessory Nerve (CN XI)
• Origin: spinal cord C1–C5
• Motor → sternocleidomastoid (SCM) + trapezius
• Spinal roots ascend through foramen magnum
• Exits skull through jugular foramen
• SCM → rotates head to opposite side
• Trapezius → elevates shoulder
CN XI → SCM + trapezius → head rotation + shoulder elevation
Champney. ECNA, 2016.
Thieme

Accessory Nerve Lesion
• Ipsilateral SCM weakness
• Difficulty turning head away from the lesion
• Ipsilateral trapezius weakness
• Weak shoulder shrug on affected side
• May produce shoulder droop
Addas, Clarke. Encyclopedia of the Neurological Sciences. 2003.
CN XI lesion → weak ipsilateral shoulder shrug + difficulty turning head contralaterally

Hypoglossal Nerve (CN XII)
• Origin: medulla
• General somatic efferent (GSE)
• Motor to intrinsic + extrinsic tongue muscles
• Exception: palatoglossus → CN X
• Exits skull through hypoglossal canal
• Genioglossus protrudes the tongue
CN XII = motor to tongue | Palatoglossus = CN X
Singh. TBCNA, 3e.
Champney. ECNA, 2016.

Hypoglossal Lesions: UMN vs LMN
LMN / CN XII Lesion
• Ipsilateral tongue weakness
• Atrophy + fasciculations
• Tongue deviates toward the lesion on protrusion
UMN / Corticobulbar Lesion
• Contralateral genioglossus weakness
• No prominent atrophy/fasciculations
• Tongue deviates away from the cortical lesion
LMN → toward lesion | UMN → away from lesion
The tongue deviates toward the weak genioglossus

Tongue Innervation
Anterior 2/3
• General sensation (GSA): lingual n. (CN V3)
• Taste (SVA): chorda tympani (CN VII)
Posterior 1/3
• General sensation (GSA): CN IX
• Taste (SVA): CN IX
Most Posterior Tongue & Epiglottis
• General sensation + taste: CN X
Motor
• CN XII: intrinsic + extrinsic tongue muscles
• Exception: palatoglossus → CN X

Internal Organization of the Brainstem
Long Tracts • Cross-Sections • Vascular Territories

Major Long Tracts Through the Brainstem
Corticospinal Dorsal Column Spinothalamic
Tract (proprioception and vibration) (pain and temperature)
• Corticospinal tract → voluntary motor control
• Medial lemniscus → fine touch, vibration, proprioception
• Spinothalamic tract → pain & temperature
In the brainstem, these pathways have already
crossed or will cross at predictable levels.
LMN: lower motor neuron
UMN: upper motor neuron
WB, NA

Long Tracts in the Brainstem
Corticospinal Tract
• Crosses in caudal medulla
• Brainstem lesion above crossing → contralateral weakness
Medial Lemniscus
• Crosses in caudal medulla
• Brainstem lesion above crossing → contralateral loss of fine touch, vibration & proprioception
Spinothalamic Tract
• Already crossed in spinal cord
• Brainstem lesion → contralateral loss of pain & temperature

Face vs Body Sensory Pathways
Face
• Principal sensory nucleus of V → fine touch/vibration
• Spinal trigeminal nucleus/tract → pain & temperature
Body
• Medial lemniscus → fine touch/vibration/proprioception
• Spinothalamic tract → pain & temperature
Brainstem lesion may produce ipsilateral face + contralateral body deficits

How to Read a Brainstem Cross-Section
Identify the level
• Midbrain | pons | medulla
Find orientation landmarks:
• Aqueduct | 4th ventricle | colliculi | olive/pyramids
Identify CN nuclei/fascicles:
• Which cranial nerves belong at this level?
Locate major long tracts:
• Corticospinal | medial lemniscus | spinothalamic
Orient medial vs lateral:
• Prepare to localize lesions
Cross-Section of Central Medulla
Landmark → CN structures → Long tracts → Medial/Lateral

Landmarks

Midbrain: Inferior Colliculus Level
Landmarks

Inferior colliculus + CN IV → caudal midbrain
Fig. 11.3. Siegel, EN, 4e.

Landmarks

Fig. 10.6. Siegel, EN, 4e.

Middle Pons
Landmarks
• 4th ventricle

CN Nuclei
• Principal sensory nucleus of CN V
• Motor nucleus of CN V
Long Tracts

CN V nuclei → mid-pons
Other Key Structures

Fig. 10.5. Siegel, EN, 4e.

Caudal Pons
Landmark
• Facial colliculus
• 4th ventricle
CN Nuclei

• Vestibular nuclei (CN VIII)

Fig. 10.4. Siegel, EN, 4e.

Upper (Open) Medulla
Landmarks
• 4th ventricle
• Inferior olive
CN/Sensory Nuclei

Cerebellar Connection Olive + open 4th ventricle → rostral/open medulla

Fig. 9.8. Siegel, EN, 4e.

Central Medulla
Landmarks
• 4th ventricle
• Inferior olive
CN Nuclei
• Hypoglossal nucleus (CN XII)

• Nucleus ambiguus

Long Tracts
• Pyramid → corticospinal tract

Cerebellar Connection
Medial structures → XII + pyramid + medial lemniscus
• Inferior cerebellar peduncle
Lateral structures → ambiguus + spinal V + spinothalamic
Fig. 9.8. Siegel, EN, 4e.

Lower (Closed) Medulla
Landmark
• Central canal
Sensory Structures
• Gracile + cuneate nuclei
• Internal arcuate fibers → sensory decussation
• Formation of medial lemniscus
Motor Structure
• Pyramids
• Pyramidal decussation
Face/Body Pain Pathways
• Spinal trigeminal nucleus & tract
• Spinothalamic tract
Caudal medulla = two major crossings: sensory decussation + pyramidal decussation
Fig. 9.3. Siegel, EN, 4e.
